script: Good morning, and welcome to Wren Lane Glassworks. I'm Martin, and I've been restoring stained-glass windows here for nearly twenty years.
Before we begin, I should mention that the tour lasts about forty minutes, and photography is allowed everywhere except in the cutting room, where we need everyone's full attention on safety.
The building itself was originally a school.

It was turned into a workshop in the nineteen-sixties, when the old craft company that owned it needed more light for its work. The tall windows that made the classrooms bright are exactly what glass painters need.
Most of our work today is restoration rather than new design.

About four out of every five projects come from churches, but we also repair windows from private houses and, increasingly, from old railway stations. Those are often the most interesting jobs, because the glass has usually been hidden under decades of smoke and dirt.
People often think the hardest part of restoration is matching the colour of old glass. In fact, we can usually find or make a close match.
What really takes time is removing the old lead that holds the pieces together without cracking the glass next to it.

In this first room you'll see our largest current project. It's a window from a seaside chapel which was damaged not by vandals, as the newspapers reported, but by salt carried on the wind over more than a century.
Next door is the painting studio.
The painters here use a mixture of ground glass and metal oxides, which is then fired in a kiln so that it becomes part of the surface.
That's why good stained glass doesn't fade the way paint on a wall does.
Our apprentices train for four years. In the first year they mostly cut and clean glass; they don't start painting until the third year.
At the end of the tour you'll reach our shop. All the small pieces sold there are made from offcuts, the leftover glass from larger projects, so nothing goes to waste.
Finally, on the last Friday of each month we run a taster class for adults. It's very popular, so I'd recommend booking at least six weeks in advance.

paragraphs: A. For most of its long history, window glass has had a single job: to let light in while keeping the weather out. A window was a passive object, and the only choice an architect really made was how large it should be. That is now changing. A new generation of so-called smart glass can alter how much light and heat passes through it, either automatically or at the press of a button, and its supporters argue that it could transform the way buildings use energy.

B. The reason for the interest is simple. In many office buildings, windows are the weakest point in the building's defence against heat. On a summer afternoon, sunlight pouring through a glass wall can raise indoor temperatures so quickly that air-conditioning systems must work at full power. In winter, the same glass allows warmth to escape. Engineers estimate that in a typical glass-fronted office, heating and cooling linked to the windows can account for a significant share of the building's total energy bill.

C. Smart glass comes in several forms. The most widely used type, known as electrochromic glass, contains extremely thin layers of material that darken when a small electrical current is applied. A second type, thermochromic glass, needs no electricity at all; it darkens by itself as it warms up. Each has its drawbacks. Electrochromic panels can take up to twenty minutes to change from clear to dark, which can frustrate occupants who want an immediate response. Thermochromic glass, meanwhile, reacts to its own temperature rather than to the needs of the people inside, so it may darken on a cold but sunny day when the warmth would actually be welcome.

D. Early trials have produced encouraging results. In one study of a renovated university library, replacing ordinary windows with electrochromic panels reduced the energy used for cooling by around a fifth over two years. Just as importantly, staff reported less glare on their computer screens, and fewer people kept their blinds permanently closed. The library's director said the change had made the reading rooms feel noticeably larger, even though nothing else about them had changed. The researchers pointed out that blinds, although cheap, often defeat the purpose of large windows, since they block the daylight and the view along with the heat.

E. Cost, however, remains the main obstacle. Smart glass can be several times more expensive than high-quality conventional double glazing, and the savings on energy bills may take many years to cover the difference. For this reason, the technology has so far been adopted mainly in prestige projects such as airports, headquarters buildings and hospitals, where the owners are prepared to pay extra for comfort and a modern image.

F. There are also questions about durability. Ordinary glass can last for decades with little attention, but the coatings and electronics in smart windows are newer, and manufacturers can only estimate how they will perform after thirty or forty years. Repairs can also be complicated, because a fault in the wiring may require specialist technicians rather than an ordinary glazier. Some building managers worry that a single failed panel could leave one part of a facade permanently darker than the rest, and that replacement panels might not match the originals.

G. Even so, many specialists believe the outlook is positive. As production increases, prices are expected to fall, as they did for solar panels. Some researchers are also experimenting with glass that can generate a small amount of electricity while it is dark, which could one day allow windows to power their own switching. If that happens, the humble window may finally become an active part of a building's energy system rather than its biggest weakness.

script: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for coming to the Northfield Sleep Clinic open day. I'm Dr Hannah Reid, and I lead the team here.

Let me start with who we see. Many people imagine that our patients are mostly older adults, but in fact the largest group is people in their thirties and forties, often with demanding jobs and young families.
The most common problem we treat is not snoring, as many visitors guess, but insomnia, meaning difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep.
Patients are usually referred to us by their family doctor. We do accept people who contact us directly, but the waiting time is longer.
During your tour you'll see one of our bedrooms. We've tried to make them feel like a hotel room rather than a hospital ward, because people sleep more naturally when they feel relaxed.

Each patient wears a few small sensors overnight. The one that people find most uncomfortable at first is the band around the chest, which measures breathing. The sensors on the head are actually hardly noticed.

I'd like to say a word about phones. We used to ban them completely in the bedrooms. Now we let patients keep them, but we ask them to switch them to flight mode, because a complete ban made some people too anxious to sleep.

One of the treatments we're best known for is a six-week course of talking therapy for insomnia. It doesn't involve medication, and our results show that most patients sleep better after it than they do with sleeping tablets.
We also run a free evening talk once a month, which is aimed at parents of teenagers. Teenagers naturally want to go to bed later, and parents often find it useful to understand why.
The clinic café is on the ground floor. I should warn you that it doesn't sell coffee after four o'clock. That's not an accident!
Finally, if you'd like to take part in our research, please leave your details with my colleague at the main entrance before you leave.

paragraphs: A. For centuries, sleep was regarded as a period when the brain simply switched off, a necessary but unproductive break from the business of thinking. Over the past few decades, however, researchers have built up a very different picture. The sleeping brain, it now appears, is extremely busy, and one of its most important tasks is to sort and store the experiences of the previous day. Understanding how this happens has become one of the most active areas of brain science, attracting psychologists, doctors and computer scientists alike.

B. Evidence for this idea first came from simple learning experiments. Volunteers would be taught a list of word pairs or a short sequence of finger movements in the evening and tested the following morning. Those who had slept normally performed noticeably better than those who had been kept awake through the night, even when the sleep-deprived group was allowed to rest the next day before the test. It seemed that sleep did more than protect memories from interference; it actively strengthened them. Similar improvements were later found for a wide range of skills, from learning vocabulary in a foreign language to playing short pieces on the piano.

C. Later work suggested that different stages of sleep may play different roles. During deep sleep, which dominates the early part of the night, recordings of brain activity show slow, regular waves. Many scientists believe that these waves help to transfer new information from the hippocampus, a region that holds memories temporarily, to the outer layers of the brain, where they can be kept for much longer. The lighter stage known as REM sleep, when most vivid dreaming takes place, is more often linked with emotional memories and with finding connections between separate pieces of information.

D. One of the most striking findings concerns problem-solving. In a well-known type of experiment, participants are given a mathematical task that contains a hidden shortcut. People who sleep between two attempts at the task are far more likely to discover the shortcut than people who spend the same amount of time awake. Researchers are careful to point out, though, that sleep does not produce new knowledge out of nothing; it appears to reorganise what has already been learned. In other words, the shortcut must already be present in the material; sleep simply makes it easier for the brain to notice it.

E. These results have obvious implications for students. Staying up all night before an examination may feel productive, but the research suggests it is one of the least effective ways to prepare. Material studied in short sessions spread over several days, with normal sleep in between, tends to be remembered far better. A few schools have experimented with later start times for teenagers, whose natural sleep patterns shift towards later bedtimes, and some have reported small improvements in attendance.

F. There is also growing interest in whether memory during sleep can be deliberately improved. In some laboratory studies, quiet sounds linked to information learned earlier were played to volunteers while they were in deep sleep, and recall of that information improved slightly. However, the effects so far have been modest, and the equipment involved is far from suitable for home use. Several companies have nevertheless begun advertising devices that claim to improve learning overnight, and scientists warn that most of these products have never been properly tested.

G. Not every question has been settled. Some researchers argue that the benefits of sleep have been exaggerated, pointing out that a short period of quiet rest while awake can also help memory in certain tasks. What is clear is that sleep is not wasted time. For anyone hoping to learn something new, a good night's sleep may be as valuable as an extra hour of study, and possibly a great deal more valuable than a sleepless night spent with a textbook.

script: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Ashby Gorge Bridge. My name's Ruth, and I'll be your guide for the walk across and back, which should take around an hour.
Before we set off, please note that cyclists share the path with us, so do keep to the left-hand side.

The bridge was opened in eighteen sixty-four, but the idea for it was much older. The first design was rejected because it would have cost too much, and it took more than thirty years to raise the money.
Many people believe the bridge was designed by a famous railway engineer, but in fact it was the work of a much less well-known man, a local architect who had never built a bridge before.
It's a suspension bridge, which means the road hangs from chains rather than resting on arches. The chains were originally made from iron recovered from an older bridge in London.

You may notice that the bridge moves slightly in strong winds. That's completely normal, and it's designed to do so. What does cause problems is heat: on very hot days the chains expand, and the road can drop by several centimetres.
Today the bridge carries about four thousand vehicles a day. To protect it, there's a weight limit of four tonnes, which is why you won't see any buses or lorries here.
Maintenance is paid for by a small toll, which car drivers pay at the eastern end. Pedestrians and cyclists cross for free.
Halfway across, we'll stop at the viewing point. From there you can see the river two hundred feet below, and if you're lucky, the peregrine falcons that nest on the cliffs.
At the far side there's a visitor centre. The most popular exhibit there isn't the model of the bridge, but a collection of photographs taken by the engineer's daughter during construction.

paragraphs: A. Undersea tunnels are among the most ambitious structures ever attempted by engineers. Unlike a bridge, which is visible from miles away, a tunnel beneath the sea is almost entirely hidden, and the public rarely appreciates the difficulty of building one. Yet tunnels have advantages that bridges cannot match. They are unaffected by storms and fog, they leave shipping lanes open, and they do not spoil coastal views. For these reasons, governments planning to link islands or coastlines have increasingly chosen to go under the water rather than over it, even though tunnels generally take longer to plan and build.

B. There are two main ways to build such a tunnel. The first is to bore through the rock beneath the seabed using enormous tunnel-boring machines. These machines, which can be longer than a football pitch, cut through the ground at the front while placing curved concrete segments behind them to form the tunnel wall. The second method, known as an immersed tube, involves building huge concrete sections on land, floating them out to sea, and sinking them into a trench dug in the seabed, where they are joined together and covered over. Each section may weigh as much as a large ship, and positioning it accurately on the seabed is a delicate operation that can be carried out only in calm weather.

C. The choice between the two depends largely on geology. Boring works best through solid, uniform rock, such as chalk, which is relatively soft but holds water out well. Where the seabed consists of loose sand or mud, an immersed tube is usually safer and cheaper, because the trench needs to be only a few metres deep. Immersed tubes also allow a tunnel to stay close to the surface, which means the approach roads on each side do not need to descend so steeply.

D. Water is the engineer's greatest enemy, both during construction and long after the tunnel opens. Even a small leak can become dangerous under the pressure of the sea above, and on some early projects workers had to breathe compressed air to keep water out of the working area, a practice that caused serious illness. Modern boring machines are sealed against the surrounding ground, so workers can operate in normal air pressure. The joints between immersed sections are fitted with thick rubber seals which are squeezed tight by the weight of the water itself.

E. Safety for users is just as important as safety during construction. Long tunnels usually contain a separate service tunnel running alongside the main one, connected at regular intervals by cross-passages. In an emergency, drivers or passengers can escape into the service tunnel, which is kept at a slightly higher air pressure so that smoke cannot enter it. Ventilation is another major concern, especially in road tunnels, where vehicle fumes must be removed continuously by powerful fans.

F. Undersea tunnels are extremely expensive, and many have cost far more than originally planned. Critics argue that the money might be better spent on improving ferry services, which are flexible and can be expanded gradually. Supporters reply that tunnels last for well over a century and that their value should be judged over that period rather than over the first few years of operation, when traffic is often lower than forecast. They also point to the economic benefits for towns at either end, which may find themselves suddenly within easy reach of much larger markets.

script: Welcome to the Desert House at Fernhill Botanical Gardens. I'm Sam, one of the gardeners, and I'll be showing you around for the next half hour.

The first thing most visitors notice is the heat. In fact, the temperature in here is only about twenty-eight degrees during the day. What makes it feel hotter is the bright light coming through the glass roof.

People often ask how often we water the plants. In summer it's roughly once every two weeks. In winter, when many of these plants are resting, we hardly water them at all.
The biggest danger to a desert plant in a glasshouse isn't drought. It's too much water, which causes the roots to rot. That's why visitors are asked never to pour their drinks into the beds.
On your left is our oldest cactus. It's about ninety years old, and it's only been moved once, when the house was rebuilt in the nineteen-eighties. Moving it took eight people and a whole day.

paragraphs: A. In some of the driest places on Earth, there is water in the air even when it almost never rains. Along parts of the coasts of Chile, Peru, Morocco and Namibia, cold ocean currents cool the air above them, and thick fogs drift inland on most mornings of the year. For local communities, many of which depend on water delivered by truck at great expense, these fogs represent an untapped resource. Over the past few decades, a simple technology known as fog harvesting has been developed to capture some of this moisture. Although the idea sounds modern, people in several dry regions have long known that trees and stones collect water on foggy mornings.

B. The basic principle is straightforward. A large sheet of fine plastic mesh, typically several metres wide, is stretched between two posts and placed facing the direction of the wind. As fog passes through the mesh, tiny droplets of water collide with the fibres and stick to them. Gradually these droplets merge into larger drops, which become heavy enough to run down the mesh into a gutter at the bottom. From there, the water is carried through pipes to storage tanks, often without the need for any pumps or electricity, since gravity alone moves the water downhill to the villages below.

C. The amount of water collected varies enormously. On a good site, a single large net may yield several hundred litres on a foggy day, but on other days it may produce almost nothing. Location is therefore critical. Engineers usually spend at least a year testing a site with small experimental collectors before installing full-sized nets, measuring not only how often fog occurs but also the speed of the wind and the size of the droplets. Hillsides at a moderate height, where the fog is thickest, generally give the best results.

D. Fog harvesting has some clear advantages. The equipment is cheap compared with wells or desalination plants, and it can be built and repaired by local people with simple tools. The water is usually clean enough to drink after basic treatment, and because the system has no moving parts, it can work for years with little maintenance. In one village project in Morocco, collected water was piped directly to households, and women and girls no longer had to spend several hours a day fetching water from distant wells. Teachers in the area reported that more girls began attending school regularly once the daily journey was no longer necessary.

E. However, the technology is not without problems. Nets can be torn by strong winds, and in some early projects they were damaged faster than communities could replace them. Success also depends on local commitment. Several projects declined after the outside organisations that had installed them left, because no one had been trained to manage repairs or to collect small payments for maintenance. Researchers now emphasise that community ownership is as important as engineering, and many new projects now include a local committee from the very beginning.

F. Scientists are also trying to improve the mesh itself. Some designs copy the surface of a desert beetle found in Namibia, whose back has a pattern of water-attracting bumps surrounded by water-repelling areas, allowing it to drink from the fog. Other researchers have found that using harp-like vertical wires instead of a woven mesh can significantly increase the amount of water collected, because drops slide down more easily without blocking the gaps.

G. Fog harvesting will never solve the water problems of entire cities, and it only works in places where fog is frequent. But for small, isolated communities in the right locations, it offers a low-cost and sustainable supply, and it demonstrates that some of the best solutions to environmental problems are also among the simplest.

paragraphs: A. Walk through any forest and you will see trees, shrubs and perhaps the occasional mushroom. What you will not see is the vast network of fungal threads spreading through the soil beneath your feet. These threads, called hyphae, are often finer than a human hair, yet together they may stretch for many kilometres in a single handful of forest soil. Over the past thirty years, scientists have come to believe that this hidden network plays a central role in the life of the forest.

B. Most of the world's plants form partnerships with fungi known as mycorrhizae. In this relationship, the fungus wraps around or enters the plant's roots. The fungus is very good at absorbing water and minerals such as phosphorus from the soil, and it passes some of these to the plant. In return, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars that it produces through photosynthesis. Neither partner is entirely dependent on the other, but both usually grow better together than apart.

C. The idea that has attracted the most public attention is that these fungal networks connect different trees to one another. Laboratory and field experiments using carbon that can be traced have shown that sugars can move from one tree to another through shared fungal threads. This discovery led some researchers to describe the forest as a cooperative community, in which large, older trees support young seedlings growing in deep shade, where there is too little light for them to make enough food themselves.

D. The image of a so-called wood wide web, through which trees share food and even send warning signals, has become extremely popular. It has appeared in best-selling books, documentaries and even films. Many readers have been attracted to the idea that forests behave rather like families, with older trees caring for their offspring. For many people, the idea has also become a powerful argument for protecting old forests rather than replacing them with new plantations.

E. However, a number of scientists have recently warned that the popular story has run ahead of the evidence. In a widely discussed review, a team of forest ecologists examined the main field studies and concluded that many of them were small, difficult to repeat, or open to other explanations. For example, sugars might pass between trees through the soil itself rather than through connected fungi. The reviewers did not claim that fungal networks are unimportant; rather, they argued that claims about trees deliberately helping each other were not yet supported by strong data.

F. Part of the difficulty lies in the nature of the subject. Fungal networks are almost impossible to observe directly without disturbing them, because digging up the soil destroys the very connections researchers want to study. Experiments in pots or greenhouses are easier to control, but conditions there are very different from those in a real forest, where thousands of species of plants and fungi interact at the same time.

G. Whatever the final verdict on tree cooperation, the practical importance of mycorrhizal fungi is not in doubt. Foresters have found that young trees planted in damaged or heavily farmed soil often grow poorly until suitable fungi become established. Some tree nurseries now add fungi to the soil of seedlings before planting, and early results suggest this can improve survival rates, particularly on difficult sites.

H. The debate also has a wider lesson. Scientific ideas can become popular very quickly when they offer an attractive story, but popularity is not the same as proof. For the moment, the forest floor remains one of the least understood environments on the planet, and many of its secrets are still waiting to be uncovered by patient researchers willing to look beneath the surface.

paragraphs: A. Ask a group of adults whether the years seem to pass more quickly than they did in childhood, and most will say yes. A summer holiday that once felt endless now seems to disappear in a few weeks, and birthdays appear to arrive with alarming frequency. This feeling is so common that it is often treated as a simple fact of life. Psychologists, however, have spent decades trying to understand why it happens, and their explanations reveal a great deal about how the mind measures time.

B. One of the oldest explanations is mathematical. For a five-year-old, a single year represents a fifth of everything the child has experienced, whereas for a fifty-year-old it is only a fiftieth. According to this theory, each year feels shorter because it is a smaller proportion of a person's life. The idea is attractive in its simplicity, but critics point out that it does not explain why a single boring afternoon can still feel extremely long to an adult.

C. A second explanation focuses on memory. When we look back on a period of time, we tend to judge its length by the number of distinct memories it contains. Childhood is full of new experiences, such as the first day at school, the first trip abroad or the first time riding a bicycle, and each of these creates a strong memory. Adult life, by contrast, often settles into routines, and weeks that are much the same leave few separate memories behind. Looking back, such periods seem to have passed quickly.

D. This explanation also helps to account for a curious paradox. A holiday in a new place often feels as if it is passing very fast while it is happening, yet when we remember it later it seems to have lasted a long time. A dull week at work has the opposite effect: it drags while we are living it, but almost disappears in memory. Researchers sometimes call this the holiday paradox, and it suggests that the experience of time is shaped by two different processes.

E. Attention also plays a role. Experiments show that when people are asked to concentrate on the passing of time, for example by waiting for a signal, the minutes seem to stretch. When they are absorbed in a demanding task, they often underestimate how much time has passed. Some scientists have suggested that as people grow older, they become more distracted by responsibilities, and so pay less attention to time itself, although this idea has been difficult to test.

F. Physical changes may contribute as well. Some studies have found that older adults tend to estimate short intervals, such as a minute, as shorter than younger adults do, possibly because certain processes in the brain slow down with age. The evidence for this, however, is mixed, and the differences observed in laboratories are generally small. It is also unclear whether such small differences in judging a single minute could explain the much larger feeling that whole years are rushing past.

G. If routine makes time seem to vanish, then the remedy may be novelty. Psychologists suggest that adults who regularly try new activities, visit unfamiliar places or learn new skills may experience their years as fuller and longer. This does not require dramatic changes; even taking a different route to work or meeting new people can add variety to memory and give the weeks more distinct shapes when we look back on them.

H. Time, in the end, is not only measured by clocks. It is also something that the mind constructs, using memory, attention and emotion. Understanding this may not slow down the calendar, but it can help people make the time they have feel more meaningful.

paragraphs: A. Volunteering has long been regarded as one of the foundations of community life. In many countries, unpaid helpers run sports clubs, support hospitals, staff charity shops and organise local festivals. Without them, a large number of public services would either cost far more or disappear altogether. Yet in recent years, organisations that depend on volunteers have reported that it is becoming harder to recruit and keep them, and researchers have begun to ask whether the nature of volunteering itself is changing.

B. Surveys in several countries suggest that the proportion of adults who volunteer regularly, for example every week or every month, has fallen gradually over the past two decades. However, the same surveys show that occasional volunteering, such as helping at a single event, has remained stable or even increased. In other words, people have not necessarily become less generous with their time; instead, many appear to prefer shorter and more flexible forms of commitment.

C. Several explanations have been offered for this shift. Working hours have become less predictable for many people, making it difficult to promise the same time each week. Families in which both parents work have less free time than in the past. In addition, many volunteer roles now require training, forms and background checks, which can discourage people who simply want to help when they are able to. Volunteer managers report that some applicants give up while waiting for these checks to be completed.

D. Organisations have responded in different ways. Some have introduced so-called micro-volunteering, tasks that can be completed in a few minutes, often online. Examples include transcribing old documents for museums, translating short texts or identifying animals in photographs taken by wildlife cameras. Supporters argue that micro-volunteering allows people to contribute who would otherwise not take part at all. Critics, however, worry that it lacks the personal contact that makes traditional volunteering so valuable to communities.

E. There is strong evidence that volunteering benefits the volunteers themselves. Studies have linked regular volunteering with higher levels of life satisfaction and lower levels of loneliness, particularly among older people who have recently retired. One long-term study found that older volunteers were more likely to remain physically active. Researchers stress, though, that it is difficult to separate cause and effect: healthier and happier people may simply be more likely to volunteer in the first place.

F. Young people's attitudes to volunteering are also attracting attention. Many schools and universities now encourage or require students to volunteer, partly because employers value the skills it develops, such as teamwork and communication. Some observers fear that required volunteering may feel like an obligation rather than a choice, but there is some evidence that students who begin volunteering in this way often continue after the requirement ends.

G. Technology has changed not only what volunteers do but also how they are found. Online platforms now match people with local opportunities according to their skills and the hours they have available, rather like a job website. Charities that use these platforms report that they attract a younger and more varied group of volunteers than traditional advertising did. Some platforms also allow volunteers to record their hours and receive certificates, which many younger users find useful when applying for courses or jobs.

H. The future of volunteering is therefore likely to be more varied than its past. Long-term commitments will remain essential for some roles, such as mentoring a child or coaching a team, where trust takes time to build. But organisations that offer flexible opportunities, and make it easy for people to help in small ways, may find that the willingness to give time is as strong as ever, even if it is expressed in new ways.

script: Hello, and welcome to Pennick Water Mill. I'm Tom, the miller here, and I'll be showing you how we turn wheat into flour, much as it was done two hundred years ago.

paragraphs: A. For most of the twentieth century, the story of wheat was a story of rising yields. Plant breeders developed varieties that produced more grain per hectare, had shorter stems that did not fall over in the wind, and responded well to chemical fertilisers. These modern wheats helped to feed rapidly growing populations, and they now dominate farming across much of the world. Yet in recent years, a small but growing number of farmers and bakers have turned their attention to much older grains, many of which had almost disappeared from fields. Their reasons range from flavour and nutrition to concerns about the environment and the loss of traditional farming knowledge.

B. The term ancient grains is used loosely, but it usually refers to cereals that have changed little over thousands of years. Among wheats, the best-known examples are einkorn, emmer and spelt, which were grown by some of the earliest farmers in the Middle East and Europe. Other crops sometimes included under the same label, such as quinoa and millet, are not wheats at all, and some are not even true cereals. Quinoa, for instance, is more closely related to spinach than to wheat.

C. Part of the appeal of these grains is their flavour. Bakers who use them often describe the bread as nuttier or richer than bread made from modern white flour. Ancient grains are also popular with consumers who are interested in traditional food and who are willing to pay higher prices for products they see as more natural. As a result, flour made from spelt or emmer can sell for several times the price of ordinary flour.

D. Claims about health benefits are more controversial. Some studies have found that certain ancient wheats contain higher levels of particular minerals or proteins than modern varieties. However, much of the difference disappears when ancient grains are compared with modern wholemeal flour, which also contains the nutritious outer layers of the grain. Nutrition experts also warn that ancient wheats contain gluten, and so they are not suitable for people with coeliac disease, despite what some advertising suggests.

E. For farmers, ancient grains offer both opportunities and risks. Their yields are much lower, sometimes less than half those of modern wheat, so they can be profitable only if they are sold at a premium. On the other hand, they often need fewer fertilisers and can grow on poorer soils where modern wheat performs badly. Some varieties also have tough outer husks that protect the grain from insects and disease.

F. Those husks, however, create an extra problem. Unlike modern wheat, whose grain falls free during harvesting, einkorn, emmer and spelt must go through an additional process to remove the husk before milling. This requires specialist equipment, which many small farms do not own, and it adds to the final cost of the flour. In some regions, groups of farmers have shared the cost of buying a single machine, which they take turns to use after each harvest.

G. Researchers are now exploring whether the qualities of ancient grains could be combined with the high yields of modern varieties. Some breeding programmes are crossing old and new wheats in the hope of producing plants that are both productive and better able to cope with drought, which is expected to become more frequent as the climate changes. Such work is slow, however, and it may take many years before new varieties are ready for farmers to grow.

H. It is unlikely that ancient grains will ever replace modern wheat as a major food source; their low yields make that impossible. But their revival has encouraged a wider interest in crop diversity, and it reminds us that the varieties abandoned by earlier generations may still hold valuable lessons for the future of farming.

script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hollin Hill Weather Station. I'm Priya, and I'm one of the two scientists who work here.
This station has been recording the weather every day since eighteen ninety-two, which makes it one of the longest continuous records in the country.

Today, almost all the measurements are taken automatically. The only reading we still take by hand every morning is the depth of any snow on the ground, because the machines aren't reliable enough for that.
Let's start with the instrument most people recognise: the wind vane on the mast up there. It shows wind direction. Next to it is the cup anemometer, which measures wind speed.
The mast is ten metres tall. That's the international standard, so that our wind measurements can be compared with stations all over the world.
Over here is the white box, called a Stevenson screen. It holds the thermometers. It's painted white to reflect sunlight, and the sides are like shutters so that air can flow through.
Our highest wind speed was recorded during a storm in nineteen ninety. The gust was so strong that it broke the old anemometer, so the real figure was probably even higher.

You might think our data is mainly used for daily weather forecasts. In fact, its most important use is in climate research, because a long, unbroken record like ours shows how the climate has changed.
We also supply data to local farmers, and, perhaps surprisingly, to a nearby company that manages wind turbines.

One of the biggest threats to the station isn't the weather at all. It's the trees on the edge of the site. As they grow, they shelter the instruments and change the readings, so we have to cut them back regularly.
Before you leave, you're welcome to visit our small exhibition in the old observer's cottage.
And if you'd like to record the weather at your own school, we can lend you a set of basic instruments for a term.

Farmers, sailors and travellers depended on it for their survival, and over the centuries they developed a rich body of sayings that linked the appearance of the sky, the behaviour of animals or the time of year with the weather to come. Some of these sayings have a sound scientific basis. A red sky in the evening, for example, often indicates dry air to the west, which in many parts of the world means that fair weather is approaching. Others, however, are little more than superstition, such as the belief that the weather on one particular day will continue for the following forty days.

B. Scientific forecasting began to develop in the nineteenth century, made possible by two inventions. Reliable instruments such as the barometer allowed changes in air pressure to be measured accurately, and the telegraph allowed observations from distant places to be sent to a central office within hours. For the first time, forecasters could draw maps showing the weather across a whole region at a single moment and see storms moving from one area to another.

C. Early forecasts were often inaccurate, and they were sometimes treated with scepticism by the public. In some countries, official storm warnings were even suspended for a period after critics argued that they did more harm than good by keeping fishing boats in harbour unnecessarily. Gradually, however, as the network of observations grew and forecasters gained experience, the warnings became more reliable and public confidence increased. By the end of the century, weather forecasts were being published daily in many newspapers.

D. The most important change came in the twentieth century with the idea that the atmosphere could be described by mathematical equations. In theory, if the present state of the atmosphere was known precisely, these equations could be used to calculate its future state. The difficulty was the enormous number of calculations required. One early attempt to produce a forecast by hand took several weeks of work and was spectacularly wrong. It was only with the arrival of electronic computers in the nineteen-fifties that this approach became practical.

E. Today, weather services use some of the most powerful computers in the world. They divide the atmosphere into millions of boxes and calculate how temperature, pressure, wind and moisture will change in each one. Data from satellites, weather balloons, ships and aircraft are fed into these models several times a day. As a result, a five-day forecast today is about as accurate as a one-day forecast was around forty years ago.

F. Even so, there are limits to what can be predicted. The atmosphere is a chaotic system, which means that very small errors in the starting data can grow rapidly until they completely change the forecast. For this reason, forecasters now run their models many times with slightly different starting conditions. If most of the results agree, they can be confident; if they differ widely, the forecast is less certain, and this uncertainty can be communicated to the public as a percentage.

G. Local features also remain a challenge. Mountains, coastlines and even large cities can create their own weather, such as sudden showers or fog, which may be too small to appear in the models, even though they can have a serious effect on roads, airports and outdoor events. In these situations, the experience of human forecasters who know the area is still valuable.

H. Weather forecasting has thus travelled a long way from the sayings of farmers and sailors. Yet its basic aim is unchanged: to give people enough warning to plan their lives and protect themselves from the forces of nature.

script: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Caxton Lane Print Museum. My name's Gerald, and I worked as a printer for over forty years before I retired and began volunteering here.
The museum was founded in nineteen seventy-eight by a group of former printers who were worried that the old skills would be forgotten as computers took over.
Almost all the machines you'll see today still work. The only one we don't use is the oldest press, a wooden one from the seventeen-hundreds, because it's too fragile.
Our first room shows how type was set by hand. Each letter was a small piece of metal, and a skilled typesetter could arrange around two thousand letters an hour.
Many of the words we use today come from printing. For example, capital letters were kept in the upper case, a box above the small letters, which is why we still talk about upper case and lower case.
In the next room is our most popular machine. It's not the biggest press, as you might expect, but a small machine that prints visitors' names on a bookmark, which you can take home.
Printing was a dangerous job in the past. The main health risk wasn't the machines themselves, but the lead in the metal type, which could poison workers over many years.
Upstairs we have a collection of posters. The oldest one advertises a circus that visited the town in eighteen sixty.
We also run courses. Our evening class in letterpress printing is very popular with graphic designers, who want to understand the traditional methods behind their digital work.
The museum doesn't receive any regular funding from the government. We rely on ticket sales, the shop, and donations.
The shop sells cards and notebooks printed on our own machines. All the paper is recycled.
Please feel free to ask questions as we go round. Now, let's start with the type cases.

paragraphs: A. In the nineteen-seventies, as computers began to appear in offices, a number of business writers made a confident prediction. Within a few decades, they claimed, paper would largely vanish from working life. Documents would be written, stored and shared electronically, filing cabinets would be thrown away, and the so-called paperless office would become the norm. Half a century later, the prediction has only partly come true. Although the use of paper in offices has fallen in many countries in recent years, for a long time it actually increased, as computers and printers made it easier than ever to produce documents.

B. Researchers who studied this puzzle found that paper had qualities that early digital systems could not match. In one well-known investigation of office workers, people were observed using printed documents in very particular ways. They spread pages out across their desks to compare them, wrote notes in the margins, and kept piles of papers within reach as a kind of reminder of unfinished tasks. Paper, in other words, was not just a way of storing information but a tool for thinking.

C. The question of whether people read differently on paper and on screens has received a great deal of attention. A number of studies have found that, for long and complex texts, readers tend to understand and remember slightly more when they read on paper. The difference appears to be small for short or simple texts, and it may depend on the reader's habits. Some researchers suggest that people reading on screens are more likely to skim, perhaps because they associate screens with quick, informal reading such as messages and news.

D. Another possible explanation concerns the physical nature of a book. When reading on paper, people can feel how far they have progressed and often remember where on a page a particular piece of information appeared. This sense of place may help readers build a mental map of the text. Digital devices have tried to imitate this with page numbers and progress bars, but many readers report that the experience is not quite the same.

E. Paper also has a reputation, not always deserved, for being bad for the environment. In reality, its impact depends heavily on how it is produced. In many countries, a large proportion of paper is made from recycled fibres or from trees grown in managed plantations, where new trees are planted to replace those that are cut down. Digital technology, meanwhile, has its own environmental costs, including the energy used by data centres and the materials needed to manufacture devices.

F. None of this means that paper is likely to return to its former dominance. Electronic documents have clear advantages: they can be searched instantly, shared with many people at once and stored without taking up physical space. For many routine tasks, such as filling in forms or sending invoices, digital systems are faster and cheaper, and they reduce the risk of documents being lost.

G. What seems more likely is a long period of coexistence. Many people now move between the two, reading a report on screen but printing the sections they need to study closely, or drafting ideas in a notebook before typing them up. Even young people who have grown up with smartphones often say they prefer printed books for serious study.

H. The story of the paperless office offers a useful lesson about predictions. New technologies rarely replace older ones completely or as quickly as expected. Instead, people tend to keep using older tools for the tasks they perform best, even after a newer alternative arrives. The radio was not replaced by television, and television has not been replaced by the internet; each has found its own place.
